opus-5.5.text:
I think the effects really change shape over that kind of timescale, and it's easy to get the sign of things wrong if you only look at the first couple of years.

In the short run, the controls clearly bite. Cutting-edge AI training depends on a small number of very advanced chips and on an extraordinarily concentrated supply chain: the lithography machines, the leading fabs, the high-bandwidth memory. If you restrict access to those, you slow down how much compute a country can bring to bear on frontier models, and compute has been one of the main drivers of progress. So over a few years you'd expect a real gap to open up, or at least to be maintained.

But over ten years a few countervailing forces come in. The first is indigenous substitution. When you tell a large, technically capable country that it can't buy something it considers strategically vital, you create an enormous incentive to build it domestically. That doesn't happen overnight, because semiconductor manufacturing is perhaps the hardest industrial process humanity has ever developed. But a decade is long enough for a lot of catching up, especially at nodes a generation or two behind the frontier. So the controls may shift from "they can't get these chips" to "they're making their own, somewhat worse and more expensive ones."

The second is that algorithmic efficiency keeps improving. If the same capability can be reached with much less compute each year, a fixed compute gap matters a bit less over time, though the leading labs benefit from those improvements too, so it's more of a race than a simple erosion.

The third, and the one I think about most, is the effect on the broader strategic relationship. Export controls are partly a technical measure and partly a signal. If they're read as an attempt to permanently lock a rival out of a transformative technology, that could push both sides towards treating advanced AI as a zero-sum race, which is exactly the dynamic that makes it harder to slow down, coordinate on safety standards, or agree on limits. On the other hand, a compute lead can also buy breathing room: if one coalition is meaningfully ahead, it might feel less pressure to cut corners on safety.

So my honest view is that the controls probably do buy time, maybe several years, but the value of that time depends entirely on what we do with it. If it's spent building safety techniques, verification methods, and the kinds of international institutions that could eventually include China, it could be very valuable. If it's just spent racing faster, then we may have paid a large diplomatic cost for a temporary lead, and ended up in a more dangerous world than the one we started in.

r001.rationale: The response says export controls could incentivize China to build domestic chips, but does not suggest they would boost chipmaking capacity by protecting its chip industry.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention an invasion of Taiwan or a resulting loss of Western access to Taiwanese chip production.

fable-5.1.text:
Toby Ord: It's a really good question, and I think the honest answer is that the effects are likely to look quite different at the end of a decade than they do at the start.

In the near term, the controls are doing more or less what they were designed to do. If you restrict access to the most advanced chips and to the lithography equipment needed to make them, then you create a real gap in the amount of compute that Chinese labs can bring to bear on frontier training runs. And because the scaling of frontier systems has been so compute-intensive, that gap matters. It buys time — maybe a year, maybe a couple of years of lead at the frontier.

But I'd be cautious about assuming that advantage is stable. There are a few dynamics pulling in the other direction over a ten-year horizon.

The first is that export controls create an enormous incentive to build a domestic alternative. China has the engineering talent and the state capacity to pour resources into semiconductor manufacturing, and while catching up on the most advanced nodes is genuinely hard — the supply chain for extreme ultraviolet lithography is one of the most sophisticated things humans have built — hard is not the same as impossible over a decade. So you might expect the gap to narrow rather than widen.

The second is that the relationship between compute and capability may itself shift. If algorithmic efficiency keeps improving at the pace we've seen, then the amount of compute you need to reach a given level of capability keeps falling. That erodes the value of a raw compute advantage. You can end up in a situation where controls still restrict the quantity of chips, but the chips you can get are enough to do most of what matters.

And the third is the political dimension. Controls that are perceived as an attempt at permanent containment tend to harden attitudes and make cooperation on safety harder. I think one of the things I'd most want over the next ten years is some kind of international understanding about how the most dangerous capabilities get developed and governed, and it's harder to get there if one side feels the other is trying to lock it out of the technology entirely.

So my overall view is that export controls are a reasonable tool for buying time, but they're not a strategy in themselves. The question is what you do with the time. If it's used to get safety practices, evaluation regimes, and some form of international coordination in place, then it could end up being very valuable. If it's just used to race further ahead, then I think a lot of the benefit dissipates — and we might find ourselves ten years from now with a narrower lead, a more adversarial relationship, and not much to show for it.

r001.rationale: The response says export controls would incentivize China to build domestic alternatives, but does not say they boost chipmaking capacity by protecting the domestic industry.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention an invasion of Taiwan or loss of access to Taiwanese chip production.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether they create a lasting disadvantage or mainly buy time. Those could look quite similar in the first year or two, but very different over a decade.

In the short term, restricting access to advanced chips could slow Chinese AI development. But over ten years, you have to consider the response: greater investment in domestic chip production, attempts to find alternative suppliers, and improvements in how efficiently existing chips are used. So you shouldn’t assume that the initial effect simply persists.

And then there’s a separate question about what that delay achieves. If it gives us time to improve AI safety and develop international agreements, that could be very valuable. If it instead deepens an arms-race dynamic, where each side feels it must push ahead and cannot afford to cooperate, the consequences could be much less favourable.

So I’d be quite uncertain about the net effect over ten years. I’d want to ask both how much time the controls buy and what we actually do with that time.

r001.rationale: The response mentions greater Chinese investment in domestic chip production, but does not connect that growth to protection provided by export controls.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention a possible invasion of Taiwan or loss of Western access to Taiwanese chip production.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should be quite uncertain about that. There’s a fairly clear short-term effect: restricting access to advanced chips makes it harder for China to train the largest AI systems. But you can’t simply extrapolate that effect over ten years, because China will respond. The controls create a stronger incentive to develop domestic chip production, find alternative suppliers, and get more capability out of the hardware that’s available.

So a policy that initially slows progress could eventually lead to a more independent Chinese industry, and therefore less American influence over what happens. That doesn’t mean the controls are necessarily a mistake. A delay could be valuable, particularly if that time is used to improve AI safety and establish international agreements. But buying time isn’t the same as solving the problem.

I’d also want to distinguish maintaining a technological lead from reducing existential risk. Those objectives might overlap, but they aren’t identical. If the result is a more intense race, with each side feeling that it has to move quickly and can’t afford to cooperate, that could make things more dangerous even if the controls succeed in their immediate objective.

r001.rationale: The response says the controls could incentivize China to develop domestic chip production, but it does not say they boost capacity by protecting the domestic industry.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention an invasion of Taiwan or the West losing access to Taiwanese chip production.
